💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the fast-moving world of Natural Language Processing (NLP), we often find ourselves comparing different language models to see which one works best for specific tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that in this blog, we used PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) technique: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models) for fine-tuning the pre-trained model on the sequence classification task.
  • The main objective of this blog post is to implement LoRA fine-tuning for sequence classification tasks using three pre-trained models from Hugging Face: meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf, mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1, and roberta-large.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the fast-moving world of Natural Language Processing (NLP), we often find ourselves comparing different language models to see which one works best for specific tasks. This blog post is all about comparing three models: RoBERTa, Mistral-7b, and Llama-2-7b. We used them to tackle a common problem - classifying tweets about disasters. It is important to note that Mistral and Llama 2 are large models with 7 billion parameters. In contrast, RoBERTa-large (355M parameters) is a relatively smaller model used as a baseline for the comparison study.

Recent findings suggest that in this blog, we used PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) technique: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models) for fine-tuning the pre-trained model on the sequence classification task. LoRa is designed to significantly reduce the number of trainable parameters while maintaining strong downstream task performance.

The main objective of this blog post is to implement LoRA fine-tuning for sequence classification tasks using three pre-trained models from Hugging Face: meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf, mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1, and roberta-large.

Note: For reproducing the reported results, please check the pinned versions in the wandb reports.

It has been revealed that roBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT Approach) is an advanced variant of the BERT model proposed by Meta AI research team. BERT is a transformer-based language model using self-attention mechanisms for contextual word representations and trained with a masked language model objective. Note that BERT is an encoder only model used for natural language understanding tasks (such as sequence classification and token classification).

In a recent development, roBERTa is a popular model to fine-tune and appropriate as a baseline for our experiments. For more information, you can check the Hugging Face model card.

Llama 2 models, which stands for Large Language Model Meta AI, belong to the family of large language models (LLMs) introduced by Meta AI. The Llama 2 models vary in size, with parameter counts ranging from 7 billion to 65 billion.

Llama 2 is an auto-regressive language model, based on the transformer decoder architecture. To generate text, Llama 2 processes a sequence of words as input and iteratively predicts the next token using a sliding window. Llama 2 architecture is slightly different from models like GPT-3. For instance, Llama 2 employs the SwiGLU activation function rather than ReLU and opts for rotary positional embeddings in place of absolute learnable positional embeddings.

The recently released Llama 2 introduced architectural refinements to better leverage very long sequences by extending the context length to up to 4096 tokens, and using grouped-query attention (GQA) decoding.

Mistral 7B v0.1, with 7.3 billion parameters, is the first LLM introduced by Mistral AI. The main novel techniques used in Mistral 7B's architecture are:.

PEFT, Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning, is a collection of techniques (p-tuning, prefix-tuning, IA3, Adapters, and LoRa) designed to fine-tune large models using a much smaller set of training parameters while preserving the performance levels typically achieved through full fine-tuning.

Sources indicate that loRA, Low-Rank Adaptation, is a PEFT method that shares similarities with Adapter layers. Its primary objective is to reduce the model's trainable parameters. LoRA's operation involves learning a low rank enhancement matrix while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen.

RoBERTa has a limitatiom of maximum sequence length of 512, so we set the MAX_LEN=512 for all models to ensure a fair comparison.

According to recent reports, the data comprises a keyword, a location and the text of the tweet. For the sake of simplicity, we select the text feature as the only input to the LLM.

Sources indicate that at this stage, we prepared the train, validation, and test sets in the HuggingFace format expected by the pre-trained LLMs. The next step is to define the tokenized dataset for training using the appropriate tokenizer to transform the text feature into two Tensors of sequence of token ids and attention masks. As each model has its specific tokenizer, we will need to define three different datasets.

We start by defining the RoBERTa dataloader:.

Recent findings suggest that note: The RoBERTa tokenizer has been trained to treat spaces as part of the token. As a result, the first word of the sentence is encoded differently if it is not preceded by a white space. To ensure the first word includes a space, we set add_prefix_space=True. Also, to maintain consistent pre-processing for all three models, we set the parameter to 'True' for Llama 2 and Mistral 7b.

By applying the preprocessing function to the first example of our training dataset, we have the tokenized inputs (input_ids) and the attention mask:.

It has been revealed that note: we deleted the undesired columns from our data: id, keyword, location and text. We have deleted the text because we have already converted it into the inputs ids and the attention mask:.

In this blog post, we compared the performance of three large language models (LLMs) - RoBERTa, Mistral 7b, and Llama 2 - for disaster tweet classification using LoRa. From the performance results, we can see that RoBERTa is outperforming Mistral 7B and Llama 2 by a large margin. This raises the question about whether we really need a complex and large LLM for tasks like short-sequence binary classification?

One learning we can draw from this study is that one should account for the specific project requirements, available resources, and performance needs to choose the LLMs model to use.

Also, for relatively simple prediction tasks with short sequences base models such as RoBERTa remain competitive.

Finally, we showcase that LoRa method can be applied to both encoder (RoBERTa) and decoder (Llama 2 and Mistral 7B) models.

Introducing Prodigy-HF: a direct integration with Hugging Face

📅 07 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prodigy is an annotation tool made by Explosion, a tech giant well known as the creators of spaCy.
  • Industry observers note that to foster this customisability, Explosion has started releasing plugins.
  • Industry observers note that the first main feature is that this plugin allows you to train and re-use Hugging Face models on your annotated data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prodigy is an annotation tool made by Explosion, a tech giant well known as the creators of spaCy. It's a fully scriptable product with a large community around it. The product has many features, including tight integration with spaCy and active learning capabilities. But the main feature of the product is that it is programmatically customizable with Python.

Industry observers note that to foster this customisability, Explosion has started releasing plugins. These plugins integrate with third-party tools in an open way that encourages users to work on bespoke annotation workflows. However, one customization specifically deserves to be celebrated explicitly. Last week, Explosion introduced Prodigy-HF, which offers code recipes that directly integrate with the Hugging Face stack. It's been a much-requested feature on the Prodigy support forum, so we're super excited to have it out there.

Industry observers note that the first main feature is that this plugin allows you to train and re-use Hugging Face models on your annotated data. That means if you've been annotating data in our interface for named entity recognition, you can directly fine-tune BERT models against it.

After installing the plugin you can call the hf.train.ner recipe from the command line to train a transformer model directly on your own data.

Sources indicate that this will fine-tune the distilbert-base-uncased model for the dataset you've stored in Prodigy and save it to disk. Similarly, this plugin also supports models for text classification via a very similar interface.

This offers a lot of flexibility because the tool directly integrates with the AutoTokenizer and AutoModel classes of Hugging Face transformers. Any transformer model on the hub can be fine-tuned on your own dataset with just a single command. These models will be serialised on disk, which means that you can upload them to the Hugging Face Hub, or re-use them to help you annotate data. This can save a lot of time, especially for NER tasks. To re-use a trained NER model you can use the hf.correct.ner recipe.

This will give you a similar interface as before, but now the model predictions will be shown in the interface as well.

It has been revealed that the second feature, which is equally exciting, is that you can now also publish your annotated datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. This is great if you're interested in sharing datasets that others would like to use.

Sources indicate that we're particularly fond of this upload feature because it encourages collaboration. People can annotate their own datasets independently of each other, but still benefit when they share the data with the wider community.

In a recent development, we hope that this direct integration with the Hugging Face ecosystem enables many users to experiment more. The Hugging Face Hub offers many models for a wide array of tasks as well as a wide array of languages. We really hope that this integration makes it easier to get data annotated, even if you've got a more domain specific and experimental use-case.

More features for this library are on their way, and feel free to reach out on the Prodigy forum if you have more questions.

We'd also like to thank the team over at Hugging Face for their feedback on this plugin, specifically @davanstrien, who suggested to add the upload feature. Thanks!

Make your llama generation time fly with AWS Inferentia2

📅 07 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Update (02/2024): Performance has improved even more!
  • In a previous post on the Hugging Face blog, we introduced AWS Inferentia2, the second-generation AWS Inferentia accelerator, and explained how you could use optimum-neuron to quickly deploy Hugging Face models for standard text and vision tasks on AWS Inferencia 2 instances.
  • In a further step of integration with the AWS Neuron SDK, it is now possible to use 🤗 optimum-neuron to deploy LLM models for text generation on AWS Inferentia2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update (02/2024): Performance has improved even more! Check our updated benchmarks.

In a previous post on the Hugging Face blog, we introduced AWS Inferentia2, the second-generation AWS Inferentia accelerator, and explained how you could use optimum-neuron to quickly deploy Hugging Face models for standard text and vision tasks on AWS Inferencia 2 instances.

In a further step of integration with the AWS Neuron SDK, it is now possible to use 🤗 optimum-neuron to deploy LLM models for text generation on AWS Inferentia2.

And what better model could we choose for that demonstration than Llama 2, one of the most popular models on the Hugging Face hub.

According to recent reports, our recommendation is to use the Hugging Face Neuron Deep Learning AMI (DLAMI). The DLAMI comes with all required libraries pre-packaged for you, including the Optimum Neuron, Neuron Drivers, Transformers, Datasets, and Accelerate.

Alternatively, you can use the Hugging Face Neuron SDK DLC to deploy on Amazon SageMaker.

Note: stay tuned for an upcoming post dedicated to SageMaker deployment.

Finally, these components can also be installed manually on a fresh Inferentia2 instance following the optimum-neuron installation instructions.

As explained in the optimum-neuron documentation, models need to be compiled and exported to a serialized format before running them on Neuron devices.

Fortunately, 🤗 optimum-neuron offers a very simple API to export standard 🤗 transformers models to the Neuron format.

This deserves a little explanation:.

Depending on your choice of parameters and inferentia host, this may take from a few minutes to more than an hour.

Fortunately, you will need to do this only once because you can save your model and reload it later.

Even better, you can push it to the Hugging Face hub.

Once your model has been exported, you can generate text using the transformers library, as it has been described in detail in this previous post.

Note: when passing multiple input prompts to a model, the resulting token sequences must be padded to the left with an end-of-stream token. The tokenizers saved with the exported models are configured accordingly.

The following generation strategies are supported:.

Most logits pre-processing/filters (such as repetition penalty) are supported.

For those who like to keep it simple, there is an even simpler way to use an LLM model on AWS inferentia 2 using optimum-neuron pipelines.

But how much efficient is text-generation on Inferentia2? Let's figure out!

We have uploaded on the hub pre-compiled versions of the LLama 2 7B and 13B models with different configurations:.

Note: all models are compiled with a maximum sequence length of 2048.

The llama2 7B "budget" model is meant to be deployed on inf2.xlarge instance that has only one neuron device, and enough cpu memory to load the model.

All other models are compiled to use the full extent of cores available on the inf2.48xlarge instance.

Note: please refer to the inferentia2 product page for details on the available instances.

We created two "latency" oriented configurations for the llama2 7B and llama2 13B models that can serve only one request at a time, but at full speed.

We also created two "throughput" oriented configurations to serve up to four requests in parallel.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the models, we generate tokens up to a total sequence length of 1024, starting from 256 input tokens (i.e. we generate 256, 512 and 768 tokens).

Note: the "budget" model numbers are reported but not included in the graphs for better readability.

The encoding time is the time required to process the input tokens and generate the first output token. It is a very important metric, as it corresponds to the latency directly perceived by the user when streaming generated tokens.

We test the encoding time for increasing context sizes, 256 input tokens corresponding roughly to a typical Q/A usage, while 768 is more typical of a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) use-case.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Encoding time is expressed in seconds.

We can see that all deployed models exhibit excellent response times, even for long contexts.

The end-to-end latency corresponds to the total time to reach a sequence length of 1024 tokens.

It therefore includes the encoding and generation time.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Latency is expressed in seconds.

All models deployed on the high-end instance exhibit a good latency, even those actually configured to optimize throughput.

The "budget" deployed model latency is significantly higher, but still ok.

Recent findings suggest that we adopt the same convention as other benchmarks to evaluate the throughput, by dividing the end-to-end latency by the sum of both input and output tokens. In other words, we divide the end-to-end latency by batch_size * sequence_length to obtain the number of generated tokens per second.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Throughput is expressed in tokens/second.

Again, the models deployed on the high-end instance have a very good throughput, even those optimized for latency.

The "budget" model has a much lower throughput, but still ok for a streaming use-case, considering that an average reader reads around 5 words per-second.

We have illustrated how easy it is to deploy llama2 models from the Hugging Face hub on AWS Inferentia2 using 🤗 optimum-neuron.

The deployed models demonstrate very good performance in terms of encoding time, latency and throughput.

Interestingly, the deployed models latency is not too sensitive to the batch size, which opens the way for their deployment on inference endpoints serving multiple requests in parallel.

There is still plenty of room for improvement though:.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that latent Consistency Models (LCM) are a way to decrease the number of steps required to generate an image with Stable Diffusion (or SDXL) by distilling the original model into another version that requires fewer steps (4 to 8 instead of the original 25 to 50).
  • Recent findings suggest that we are delighted to announce a fresh method that can essentially make Stable Diffusion and SDXL faster, as if they had been distilled using the LCM process!
  • In a recent development, so, what’s the trick?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that latent Consistency Models (LCM) are a way to decrease the number of steps required to generate an image with Stable Diffusion (or SDXL) by distilling the original model into another version that requires fewer steps (4 to 8 instead of the original 25 to 50). Distillation is a type of training procedure that attempts to replicate the outputs from a source model using a latest one. The distilled model may be designed to be smaller (that’s the case of DistilBERT or the recently-released Distil-Whisper) or, in this case, require fewer steps to run. It’s usually a lengthy and costly process that requires huge amounts of data, patience, and a few GPUs.

Well, that was the status quo before today!

Recent findings suggest that we are delighted to announce a fresh method that can essentially make Stable Diffusion and SDXL faster, as if they had been distilled using the LCM process! How does it sound to run any SDXL model in about 1 second instead of 7 on a 3090, or 10x faster on Mac? Read on for details!

In a recent development, so, what’s the trick? For latent consistency distillation, each model needs to be distilled separately. The core idea with LCM LoRA is to train just a small number of adapters, known as LoRA layers, instead of the full model. The resulting LoRAs can then be applied to any fine-tuned version of the model without having to distil them separately. If you are itching to see how this looks in practice, just jump to the next section to play with the inference code. If you want to train your own LoRAs, this is the process you’d use:.

For more details on the process, please download our paper.

It has been revealed that fast inference of Stable Diffusion and SDXL enables new use-cases and workflows. To name a few:.

According to recent reports, to gauge the speed difference we are talking about, generating a single 1024x1024 image on an M1 Mac with SDXL (base) takes about a minute. Using the LCM LoRA, we get great results in just ~6s (4 steps). This is an order of magnitude faster, and not having to wait for results is a game-changer. Using a 4090, we get almost instant response (less than 1s). This unlocks the use of SDXL in applications where real-time events are a requirement.

The version of diffusers released today makes it very easy to use LCM LoRAs:.

As expected, using just 1 step produces an approximate shape without discernible features and lacking texture. However, results quickly improve, and they are usually very satisfactory in just 4 to 6 steps. Personally, I find the 8-step image in the previous test to be a bit too saturated and “cartoony” for my taste, so I’d probably choose between the ones with 5 and 6 steps in this example. Generation is so fast that you can create a bunch of different variants using just 4 steps, and then select the ones you like and iterate using a couple more steps and refined prompts as necessary.

Industry observers note that note that in the previous examples we used a guidance_scale of 1, which effectively disables it. This works well for most prompts, and it’s fastest, but ignores negative prompts. You can also explore using negative prompts by providing a guidance scale between 1 and 2 – we found that larger values don’t work.

As you can see, images in this example are pretty much useless until ~20 steps (second row), and quality still increases noticeably with more steps. The details in the final image are amazing, but it took 50 steps to get there.

This technique also works for any other fine-tuned SDXL or Stable Diffusion model. To demonstrate, let's see how to run inference on collage-diffusion, a model fine-tuned from Stable Diffusion v1.5 using Dreambooth.

LCM LoRA technique with a Dreambooth Stable Diffusion v1.5 model, allowing 4-step inference.

For cards with a lot of capacity, such as A100, performance increases significantly when generating multiple images at once, which is usually the case for production workloads.

#2438. Industry News: Open LLM Leaderboard: DROP deep dive

📅 01 Dec 2023 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1136 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Open LLM Leaderboard: DROP deep dive

📅 01 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, three new benchmarks were added to the Open LLM Leaderboard: Winogrande, GSM8k and DROP, using the original implementations reproduced in the EleutherAI Harness.
  • According to recent reports, DROP (Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs) is an evaluation where models must extract relevant information from English-text paragraphs before executing discrete reasoning steps on them (for example, sorting or counting items to arrive at the correct answer, see the table below for examples).
  • Sources indicate that we added it to the Open LLM Leaderboard three weeks ago, and observed that the f1-scores of pretrained models followed an unexpected trend: when we plotted DROP scores against the leaderboard original average (of ARC, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA and MMLU), which is a reasonable proxy for overall model performance, we expected DROP scores to be correlated with it (with better models having better performance).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, three new benchmarks were added to the Open LLM Leaderboard: Winogrande, GSM8k and DROP, using the original implementations reproduced in the EleutherAI Harness. A cursory look at the scores for DROP revealed something strange was going on, with the overwhelming majority of models scoring less than 10 out of 100 on their f1-score! We did a deep dive to understand what was going on, come with us to see what we found out!

According to recent reports, DROP (Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs) is an evaluation where models must extract relevant information from English-text paragraphs before executing discrete reasoning steps on them (for example, sorting or counting items to arrive at the correct answer, see the table below for examples). The metrics used are custom f1 and exact match scores.

Sources indicate that we added it to the Open LLM Leaderboard three weeks ago, and observed that the f1-scores of pretrained models followed an unexpected trend: when we plotted DROP scores against the leaderboard original average (of ARC, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA and MMLU), which is a reasonable proxy for overall model performance, we expected DROP scores to be correlated with it (with better models having better performance). However, this was only the case for a small number of models, and all the others had a very low DROP f1-score, below 10.

It has been revealed that during our first deeper dive in these surprising behavior, we observed that the normalization step was possibly not working as intended: in some cases, this normalization ignored the correct numerical answers when they were directly followed by a whitespace character other than a space (a line return, for example). Let's look at an example, with the generation being 10\n\nPassage: The 2011 census recorded a population of 1,001,360, and the gold answer being 10.

Normalization happens in several steps, both for generation and gold:.

However, the overall score is not computed on the string, but on the bag of words (BOW) extracted from the string, here {'recorded', 'population', 'passage', 'census', '2011.0', '1001360.0', '10'}, which is compared with the BOW of the gold, also normalized in the above manner, {10.0}. As you can see, they don’t intersect, even though the model predicted the correct output!

Recent findings suggest that in summary, if a number is followed by any kind of whitespace other than a simple space, it will not pass through the number normalization, hence never match the gold if it is also a number! This first matter was likely to mess up the scores quite a bit, but clearly it was not the only factor causing DROP scores to be so low. We decided to investigate a bit more.

Extending our investigations, our friends at Zeno joined us and undertook a much more thorough exploration of the results, looking at 5 models which were representative of the problems we noticed in DROP scores: falcon-180B and mistral-7B were underperforming compared to what we were expecting, Yi-34B and tigerbot-70B had a very good performance on DROP correlated with their average scores, and facebook/xglm-7.5B fell in the middle.

You can give analyzing the results a try in the Zeno project here if you want to!

The Zeno team found two even more concerning features:.

Industry observers note that at this point, we believed that both failure cases were actually caused by the same root factor: using . as a stopword token (to end the generations):.

It has been revealed that we hypothesized that both these problems could be fixed by using \n instead of . as an end of generation stop word.

So we gave it a try! We investigated using \n as the end of generation token on the available results. We split the generated answer on the first \n it contained, if one was present, and recomputed the scores. Note that this is only an approximation of the correct result, as it won't fix answers that were cut too early on . (for example floating point answers) - but it also won’t give unfair advantage to any model, as all of them were affected by this problem. However it’s the best we could do without rerunning models (as we wanted to keep the community posted as soon as possible).

The results we got were the following - splitting on \n correlates really well with other scores and therefore with overall performance.

A quick calculation shows that re-running the full evaluation of all models would be quite costly (the full update took 8 years of GPU time, and a lot of it was taken by DROP), we estimated how much it would cost to only re-run failing examples.

In a recent development, in 10% of the cases, the gold answer is a floating number (for example 12.25) and model predictions start with the correct beginning (for our example, 12) but are cut off on a . - these predictions likely would have actually been correct if the generation was to continue. We would definitely need to re-run them! Our estimation does not count generated sentences that finish with a number which was possibly interrupted (40% of the other generations), nor any prediction messed up by its normalization.

In a recent development, to get correct results, we would thus need to re-run more than 50% of the examples, a huge amount of GPU time! We need to be certain that the implementation we'll run is correct this time.

After discussing it with the fantastic EleutherAI team (both on GitHub and internally), who guided us through the code and helped our investigations, it became very clear that the LM Eval Harness implementation follows the "official DROP" code very strictly: a upcoming version of this benchmark’s evaluation thus needs to be developed! We have therefore taken the decision to remove DROP from the Open LLM Leaderboard until a new version arises.

Industry observers note that one take away of this investiguation is the value in having the many eyes of the community collaboratively investiguate a benchmark in order to detect errors that were previously missed. Here again the power of open-source, community and developping in the open-shines in that it allows to transparently investigate the root cause of an issue on a benchmark which has been out there for a couple of years.

In a recent development, we hope that interested members of the community will join forces with academics working on DROP evaluation to fix both its scoring and its normalization. We'd love it becomes usable again, as the dataset itself is really quite interesting and cool. We encourage you to provide feedback on how we should evaluate DROP on this concern.

Thanks to the many community members who pointed out concerns on DROP scores, and many thanks to the EleutherAI Harness and Zeno teams for their great help on this matter.

Goodbye cold boot - how we made LoRA Inference 300% faster

📅 05 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • tl;dr: We swap the Stable Diffusion LoRA adapters per user request, while keeping the base model warm allowing fast LoRA inference across multiple users.
  • In this blog we will go in detail over how we achieved that.
  • We've been able to drastically speed up inference in the Hub for public LoRAs based on public Diffusion models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

tl;dr: We swap the Stable Diffusion LoRA adapters per user request, while keeping the base model warm allowing fast LoRA inference across multiple users. You can experience this by browsing our LoRA catalogue and playing with the inference widget.

In this blog we will go in detail over how we achieved that.

We've been able to drastically speed up inference in the Hub for public LoRAs based on public Diffusion models. This has allowed us to save compute resources and provide a faster and better user experience.

To perform inference on a given model, there are two steps:.

Industry observers note that with the improvements, we were able to reduce the warm up time from 25s to 3s. We are now able to serve inference for hundreds of distinct LoRAs, with less than 5 A10G GPUs, while the response time to user requests decreased from 35s to 13s.

Let's talk more about how we can leverage some recent features developed in the Diffusers library to serve many distinct LoRAs in a dynamic fashion with one single service.

According to recent reports, loRA is a fine-tuning technique that belongs to the family of "parameter-efficient" (PEFT) methods, which try to reduce the number of trainable parameters affected by the fine-tuning process. It increases fine-tuning speed while reducing the size of fine-tuned checkpoints.

Recent findings suggest that instead of fine-tuning the model by performing tiny changes to all its weights, we freeze most of the layers and only train a few specific ones in the attention blocks. Furthermore, we avoid touching the parameters of those layers by adding the product of two smaller matrices to the original weights. Those small matrices are the ones whose weights are updated during the fine-tuning process, and then saved to disk. This means that all of the model original parameters are preserved, and we can load the LoRA weights on top using an adaptation method.

The LoRA name (Low Rank Adaptation) comes from the small matrices we mentioned. For more information about the method, please refer to this post or the original paper.

Sources indicate that the diagram above shows two smaller orange matrices that are saved as part of the LoRA adapter. We can later load the LoRA adapter and merge it with the blue base model to obtain the yellow fine-tuned model. Crucially, unloading the adapter is also possible so we can revert back to the original base model at any point.

Sources indicate that in other words, the LoRA adapter is like an add-on of a base model that can be added and removed on demand. And because of A and B smaller ranks, it is very light in comparison with the model size. Therefore, loading is much faster than loading the whole base model.

It has been revealed that if you look, for example, inside the Stable Diffusion XL Base 1.0 model repo, which is widely used as a base model for many LoRA adapters, you can see that its size is around 7 GB. However, typical LoRA adapters like this one take a mere 24 MB of space !

It has been revealed that there are far less blue base models than there are yellow ones on the Hub. If we can go promptly from the blue to yellow one and vice versa, then we have a way serve many distinct yellow models with only a few distinct blue deployments.

For a more exhaustive presentation on what LoRA is, please refer to the following blog post:Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning, or refer directly to the original paper.

Sources indicate that we have approximately 2500 distinct public LoRAs on the Hub. The vast majority (~92%) of them are LoRAs based on the Stable Diffusion XL Base 1.0 model.

Before this mutualization, this would have meant deploying a dedicated service for all of them (eg. for all the yellow merged matrices in the diagram above); releasing + reserving at least one upcoming GPU. The time to spawn the service and have it ready to serve requests for a specific model is approximately 25s, then on top of this you have the inference time (~10s for a 1024x1024 SDXL inference diffusion with 25 inference steps on an A10G). If an adapter is only occasionally requested, its service gets stopped to free resources preempted by others.

According to recent reports, if you were requesting a LoRA that was not so popular, even if it was based on the SDXL model like the vast majority of adapters found on the Hub so far, it would have required 35s to warm it up and get an answer on the first request (the following ones would have taken the inference time, eg. 10s).

Now: request time has decreased from 35s to 13s since adapters will use only a few distinct "blue" base models (like 2 significant ones for Diffusion). Even if your adapter is not so popular, there is a good chance that its "blue" service is already warmed up. In other words, there is a good chance that you avoid the 25s warm up time, even if you do not request your model that often. The blue model is already downloaded and ready, all we have to do is unload the previous adapter and load the latest one, which takes 3s as we see below.

According to recent reports, overall, this requires less GPUs to serve all distinct models, even though we already had a way to share GPUs between deployments to maximize their compute usage. In a 2min time frame, there are approximately 10 distinct LoRA weights that are requested. Instead of spawning 10 deployments, and keeping them warm, we simply serve all of them with 1 to 2 GPUs (or more if there is a request burst).

It has been revealed that we implemented LoRA mutualization in the Inference API. When a request is performed on a model available in our platform, we first determine whether this is a LoRA or not. We then identify the base model for the LoRA and route the request to a common backend farm, with the ability to serve requests for the mentioned model. Inference requests get served by keeping the base model warm and loading/unloading LoRAs on the fly. This way we can ultimately reuse the same compute resources to serve many distinct models at once.

In the Hub, LoRAs can be identified with two attributes:.

A LoRA will have a base_model attribute. This is simply the model which the LoRA was built for and should be applied to when performing inference.

Because LoRAs are not the only models with such an attribute (any duplicated model will have one), a LoRA will also need a lora tag to be properly identified.

Note that there is a more seemless way to perform the same as what is presented in this section using the peft library. Please refer to the documentation for more details. The principle remains the same as below (going from/to the blue box to/from the yellow one in the diagram above).

4 functions are used in the Diffusers library to load and unload distinct LoRA weights:.

load_lora_weights and fuse_lora for loading and merging weights with the main layers. Note that merging weights with the main model before performing inference can decrease the inference time by 30%.

unload_lora_weights and unfuse_lora for unloading.

We provide an example below on how one can leverage the Diffusers library to swiftly load several LoRA weights on top of a base model:.

All numbers below are in seconds:.

Industry observers note that with 2 to 4 additional seconds per inference, we can serve many distinct LoRAs. However, on an A10G GPU, the inference time decreases by a lot while the adapters loading time does not change much, so the LoRA's loading/unloading is relatively more expensive.

To serve inference requests, we use this open source community image.

You can find the previously described mechanism used in the TextToImagePipeline class.

When a LoRA is requested, we'll look at the one that is loaded and change it only if required, then we perform inference as usual. This way, we are able to serve requests for the base model and many distinct adapters.

Below is an example on how you can test and request this image:.

Then in another terminal perform requests to the base model and/or miscellaneous LoRA adapters to be found on the HF Hub.

Recently a really interesting paper came out, that described how to increase the throughput by performing batched inference on LoRA models. In short, all inference requests would be gathered in a batch, the computation related to the common base model would be done all at once, then the remaining adapter-specific products would be computed. We did not implement such a technique (close to the approach adopted in text-generation-inference for LLMs). Instead, we stuck to single sequential inference requests. The reason is that we observed that batching was not interesting for diffusers: throughput does not increase significantly with batch size. On the simple image generation benchmark we performed, it only increased 25% for a batch size of 8, in exchange for 6 times increased latency! Comparatively, batching is far more interesting for LLMs because you get 8 times the sequential throughput with only a 10% latency increase. This is the reason why we did not implement batching for diffusers.

It has been revealed that using dynamic LoRA loading, we were able to save compute resources and improve the user experience in the Hub Inference API. Despite the extra time added by the process of unloading the previously loaded adapter and loading the one we're interested in, the fact that the serving process is most often already up and running makes the inference time response on the whole much shorter.

In a recent development, note that for a LoRA to benefit from this inference optimization on the Hub, it must both be public, non-gated and based on a non-gated public model. Please do let us know if you apply the same method to your deployment!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing and are increasingly deployed to solve complex problems at scale.
  • Sources indicate that that's where the Optimum-NVIDIA inference library comes in.
  • According to recent reports, optimum-NVIDIA is the first Hugging Face inference library to benefit from the new float8 format supported on the NVIDIA Ada Lovelace and Hopper architectures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing and are increasingly deployed to solve complex problems at scale. Achieving optimal performance with these models is notoriously challenging due to their unique and intense computational demands. Optimized performance of LLMs is incredibly valuable for end people looking for a snappy and responsive experience, as well as for scaled deployments where improved throughput translates to dollars saved.

Sources indicate that that's where the Optimum-NVIDIA inference library comes in. Available on Hugging Face, Optimum-NVIDIA dramatically accelerates LLM inference on the NVIDIA platform through an extremely simple API. By changing just a single line of code, you can unlock up to 28x faster inference and 1,200 tokens/second on the NVIDIA platform.

According to recent reports, optimum-NVIDIA is the first Hugging Face inference library to benefit from the new float8 format supported on the NVIDIA Ada Lovelace and Hopper architectures. FP8, in addition to the advanced compilation capabilities of NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM software software, dramatically accelerates LLM inference.

You can start running LLaMA with blazingly fast inference speeds in just 3 lines of code with a pipeline from Optimum-NVIDIA. If you already set up a pipeline from Hugging Face’s transformers library to run LLaMA, you just need to modify a single line of code to unlock peak performance!

According to recent reports, you can also enable FP8 quantization with a single flag, which allows you to run a bigger model on a single GPU at faster speeds and without sacrificing accuracy. The flag shown in this example uses a predefined calibration strategy by default, though you can provide your own calibration dataset and customized tokenization to tailor the quantization to your use case.

The pipeline interface is great for getting up and running promptly, but power customers who want fine-grained control over setting sampling parameters can use the Model API.

For more details, check out our documentation.

When evaluating the performance of an LLM, we consider two metrics: First Token Latency and Throughput. First Token Latency (also known as Time to First Token or prefill latency) measures how long you wait from the time you enter your prompt to the time you begin receiving your output, so this metric can tell you how responsive the model will feel. Optimum-NVIDIA delivers up to 3.3x faster First Token Latency compared to stock transformers:.

According to recent reports, throughput, on the other hand, measures how fast the model can generate tokens and is particularly relevant when you want to batch generations together. While there are a few ways to calculate throughput, we adopted a standard method to divide the end-to-end latency by the total sequence length, including both input and output tokens summed over all batches. Optimum-NVIDIA delivers up to 28x better throughput compared to stock transformers:.

Initial evaluations of the recently announced NVIDIA H200 Tensor Core GPU show up to an additional 2x boost in throughput for LLaMA models compared to an NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU. As H200 GPUs become more readily available, we will share performance data for Optimum-NVIDIA running on them.

Optimum-NVIDIA right now provides peak performance for the LLaMAForCausalLM architecture + task, so any LLaMA-based model, including fine-tuned versions, should work with Optimum-NVIDIA out of the box today. We are actively expanding support to include other text generation model architectures and tasks, all from within Hugging Face.

We continue to push the boundaries of performance and proposal to incorporate cutting-edge optimization techniques like In-Flight Batching to improve throughput when streaming prompts and INT4 quantization to run even bigger models on a single GPU.

Recent findings suggest that give it a try: we are releasing the Optimum-NVIDIA repository with instructions on how to get started. Please share your feedback with us! 🤗.

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • In a recent development, we've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

In a recent development, we've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We declared Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

In a recent development, phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

In a recent development, it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

In a recent development, the Open TTS Leaderboard is a very latest project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a newly introduced inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

According to recent reports, phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

Recent findings suggest that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

According to recent reports, phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

In a recent development, the prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a latest one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

In a recent development, we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Industry observers note that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

In a recent development, congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

Sources indicate that one line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why.
  • To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs).
  • OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost.

To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet, the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then indicates how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet.

Figure 1. Time-series language models combine numerical measurements with text context and questions. Potential applications span physical and digital systems, with adaptation and evaluation for each task.

Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark, Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely matter, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving.

The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window.

The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs:.

Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of complications, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks.

In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the matter persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support.

According to recent reports, TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. Illustrative proactive support workflow for low disk space at Nexthink. OpenTSLM generates a state summary, a recommended action, and an expected outcome from device history and context. Spark checks the device, runs an IT-approved cleanup after employee confirmation, and follows up on the result.

Recent findings suggest that the architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path.

SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock, which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails.

Key technical benefits of SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart include:.

It has been revealed that the model in SageMaker JumpStart is OpenTSLM-Flamingo. It combines the Gemma 3 4B language model with a time-series encoder and cross-attention layers that let the language model attend to the encoded series. The model has 5.24 billion parameters in total, stored in bfloat16, so its weights take about 10.5 GB of GPU memory.

An application prepares numerical time series and text context, invokes the SageMaker endpoint, and receives the model’s response. The application can present that response to an expert or use it as input to another workflow.

This separation allows the application to control the observation window, select relevant signals, and validate the response before using it. It also makes the model independently adaptable: a newly introduced checkpoint can be evaluated against representative cases before the application switches to it.

In a recent development, in addition, we show a tutorial that fine-tunes a pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint from Hugging Face using ARFBench data loaded through TimeNet. The notebook submits a SageMaker training job that loads ARFBench through TimeNet and fine-tunes the model. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) stores the resulting model artifact, which is then deployed to a separate SageMaker real-time inference endpoint for evaluation.

According to recent reports, figure 3. A reusable architecture for deploying OpenTSLM through SageMaker JumpStart and invoking it from applications that combine time-series data with text context.

For the deployment walkthrough, use an AWS account with an Amazon SageMaker AI domain and a SageMaker AI execution role. The role must be able to create SageMaker models and endpoints in a supported Region, for example a role with the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy. The quick setup for single customers creates both. The managed policy grants broad permissions to get started. For production, use a policy that grants only the permissions you need, as described in Amazon SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples. OpenTSLM runs on a single GPU with at least 24 GB of memory and bfloat16 support, and we recommend 32 GB of host memory. The default instance type is ml.g6.2xlarge (one NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of memory, 32 GB of host memory). In SageMaker JumpStart, OpenTSLM also supports ml.g6.4xlarge, ml.g6.8xlarge, ml.g5.2xlarge, ml.g5.4xlarge, ml.g5.8xlarge, ml.g6e.xlarge, and ml.g6e.2xlarge. In the Service Quotas console, check your quota for “ml.g6.2xlarge for endpoint usage”, or for the instance type you choose. You need a quota of at least 1. If it’s lower, request an increase. See the OpenTSLM JumpStart model card for the model access requirements.

Recent findings suggest that for fine-tuning, use JupyterLab in Amazon SageMaker Studio or a local Jupyter environment with AWS credentials configured to run the accompanying notebook, which submits the training job. The notebook uses the SageMaker default S3 bucket and an execution role. Fine-tuning runs on ml.g7e.2xlarge, so also check your quota for “ml.g7e.2xlarge for training job usage”. Training runs on the job’s managed GPU instance. The notebook itself does not need a GPU. Obtain access to the selected Hugging Face checkpoint where required.

To deploy OpenTSLM in SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps:.

Figure 4: The OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B model page in SageMaker JumpStart.

Figure 5: The deploy model to endpoint form with the default ml.g6.2xlarge instance type and real-time inference.

Figure 6: The deployed OpenTSLM endpoint with InService status in SageMaker Studio.

According to recent reports, the endpoint accepts a JSON request with one or more instances. Each instance holds a question, one or more numerical series, and optional context lines. Each series has its values, a name, and a short description of the signal, such as its unit and sampling interval. A series can hold up to 32,768 values. The endpoint scales each series to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and passes the original mean and standard deviation to the model as text, so the model receives both the shape and the scale of the signal. Use None for a missing value. The model masks it.

Send the request with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to match your deployment. The calling identity needs the sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint permission. The following synthetic CPU example reveals a request.

A request can hold up to four instances, each with 1 to 32 series, and the response contains one answer per instance in generated_text. max_new_tokens accepts values from 1 to 512. The model uses greedy decoding, so the same request typically returns the same answer. A real-time invocation must complete within 60 seconds, and the request body can be up to 6 MB. On ml.g6.2xlarge, the model generates about 20 tokens per second. The endpoint processes the instances of a request in sequence, so response time grows with the number of instances and the length of the answers: an answer of 512 tokens takes about 30 seconds. To stay within 60 seconds, send several instances in one request only with short answers, for example with max_new_tokens of 128. The 6 MB limit also bounds how much series data a request can carry. For long-running requests, you can use asynchronous inference.

You can send the same request with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Save the request as JSON, for example with json.dump(request, open("request.json", "w")), then run:.

OpenTSLM-Flamingo compresses the encoded time series into a fixed-size set of representations before the language model uses it. This bounds the representation passed to the language model, but it does not make the complete system unlimited in memory or guarantee that a brief event remains easy to identify in a very long recording.

Long-context research makes this distinction concrete. TS-Haystack evaluates event retrieval across recordings of different lengths and finds that the evaluated TSLM variants often lose accuracy as the history grows, especially when locating event start and end times. These results motivate testing the chosen checkpoint on the windows and questions used by your application.

Choose a window that contains the event and enough surrounding context to interpret it. For long recordings, compare overlapping windows. Preserve sampling resolution for brief events and align related channels in time. Include units, sampling interval, and the observation period in the text context. Validate both normal and abnormal examples at the intended lengths. The endpoint’s accepted payload size and the model’s useful analysis window are separate constraints.

Follow the accompanying fine-tuning notebook for the complete example, from preparing ARFBench data with TimeNet to launching a SageMaker training job and deploying the adapted model.

Start by testing the pretrained OpenTSLM model on representative examples from your application, and assess how well it answers your questions.

Sources indicate that timeNet provides a consistent way to load the data for training and evaluation. After fine-tuning, compare the adapted model with the original on examples that were not used for training.

Sources indicate that ARFBench is a public benchmark of multiple-choice questions about anomalies in Datadog’s software-incident telemetry. We use ARFBench because its multiple-choice answers can be scored automatically, which makes the effect of fine-tuning measurable. The same workflow applies to tasks with open-ended answers, such as the summaries and recommended actions in the Nexthink example. TimeNet serves ARFBench as a versioned dataset: each question is stored with its answer options, its correct answer, and the metric signals. The training job loads ARFBench through TimeNet and the model checkpoint from Hugging Face.

A SageMaker training job runs the OpenTSLM training script on a GPU instance. The job fine-tunes the time-series encoder, the perceiver resampler, the cross-attention layers, and the language model’s token embeddings, and keeps the rest of the Gemma 3 language model frozen. The job saves the fine-tuned model to Amazon S3 in the layout of the Hugging Face model repository and writes the test accuracy before and after training to a metrics.json file. If your SageMaker Studio domain has a default MLflow App, the job also logs the training and validation loss and the test accuracy to it, so you can compare runs in the MLflow UI. In our run on one ml.g7e.2xlarge instance, accuracy on 135 held-out ARFBench questions rose from 5.0% to 45.9%. That is well above the 24.5% that random choice reaches on the full benchmark according to the ARFBench paper. Before fine-tuning, the model left most answers empty. Afterwards, it answered every question with one of the given options. ARFBench serves here as an example application: it indicates how to adapt the model to a fresh task and answer format with a public dataset. The result is not a comparison with other models or an official ARFBench leaderboard result.

Industry observers note that the following excerpt from the accompanying notebook starts the training job with ModelTrainer. scripts/train.py loads ARFBench, evaluates and fine-tunes the model, and saves it to FINETUNED_PREFIX.

According to recent reports, to deploy the fine-tuned model, create a new real-time endpoint on ml.g6.2xlarge, or another instance type that the JumpStart model supports, with the same container image and environment variables as the JumpStart model, and the inference script that the accompanying notebook provides. Point its model data to the S3 location of the fine-tuned model files. The request format stays the same, so you can send it the requests from the previous section. The accompanying notebook contains the code.

The same workflow can be adapted to other time-series tasks by pairing signal windows with relevant questions and reviewed answers. Potential examples include interpreting equipment behavior with maintenance context, explaining energy-consumption patterns with operating conditions, and describing activity from wearable measurements. The data, supervision, and evaluation should reflect the domain and the decision the application is intended to support.

Preserve the timing and meaning of the measurements during preparation, and separate training and evaluation data in a way that reflects deployment. For a predictive task, only information available at prediction time belongs in the input. Domain experts should assess whether an answer is grounded in the signals and useful for the intended workflow. For free-text answers, compare them with reviewed reference answers, for example through expert ratings or LLM-as-a-judge, where a language model scores each answer against a rubric.

Deployed endpoints continue to incur charges until you delete them. When you finish, delete the endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model. If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, run the following commands instead of choosing Delete on the endpoint page, which deletes only the endpoint. The commands look up the configuration and model names from the endpoint name and delete all three. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to the name of your endpoint, for example the default name that starts with jumpstart-dft- for a Studio deployment:.

Recent findings suggest that repeat these commands with the name of the fine-tuned endpoint. Stop the notebook application and remove tutorial-specific S3 data and artifacts that you do not intend to retain. The training job stops when it completes.

Time-series language models connect numerical measurements with the questions, context, and expertise people use to make decisions. Across manufacturing, energy, wearables, and digital infrastructure, they give people and applications a common way to interpret how systems change. The broader opportunity is to connect operational history with language, making past observations more useful in current decisions.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy it to a real-time inference endpoint in your own AWS environment through SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker SDK. TimeNet and SageMaker training jobs provide a path to adapt the model to your domain’s signals and questions.

To get started, explore Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, follow the examples in the AWS Samples repository, and consult the OpenTSLM repository and TimeNet documentation. Start with the public ARFBench example, evaluate it on representative cases, then bring the signals, questions, and expertise from your own domain.

Tech Report: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
