💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Industry observers note that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Industry observers note that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Recent findings suggest that our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a recent development, in a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

According to recent reports, left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Sources indicate that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly notable, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

Recent findings suggest that this effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

In a recent development, when we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

According to recent reports, unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

According to recent reports, this F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

In a recent development, what does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

Sources indicate that in terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

It has been revealed that notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

In a recent development, we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Industry observers note that across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

In a recent development, HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub problems autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments revealed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

It has been revealed that we created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

Recent findings suggest that this command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

In a recent development, to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

It has been revealed that HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#2427. Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1962 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications.
  • Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them.
  • Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications. That makes it an obvious place to build an AI agent. For many end customers, it is how they expect to interact with businesses. However, it is also a genuinely difficult surface to build for, even when your agent already runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The agent is rarely the hard part. The integration is. Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them. Media such as voice notes, images, and documents each require their own processing pipeline. Beyond message handling, you need conversation memory that survives sessions, durable schedules for reminders, and an authenticated path for external systems to trigger outbound messages. And anything you send more than 24 hours after the end user’s last message must use a pre-approved Meta message template.

Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them. None of it is visible to a customer, but all of it has to work. Most teams either build it from scratch or hand the integration to a third-party service.

SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is a third option: an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that gives you the full channel layer. You provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and SMART handles the rest. One command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account.

Teams are already running on SMART with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch.

Whether you are starting from scratch or migrating an existing agent, you own the agent’s logic. You let SMART handle the channel.

The following table compares what each concern costs to build yourself against what SMART provides.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. SMART builds on two of its main capabilities:.

Because AgentCore is framework-agnostic, so is SMART. Strands Agents gets memory wired automatically. LangGraph, Pydantic-AI, or another framework that gives you control over the conversation loop can integrate too. The SDK exposes the same memory and session hooks regardless of framework. You keep full control over the elements that differentiate your product: framework, model, prompt, and business logic.

The contract between SMART and your agent is deliberately small. Your agent receives the inbound message and returns text, optionally with rich message attachments. Everything else, session wiring, memory binding, delivery scheduling, is handled for you.

The following example is a complete agent.py for a SMART project. The scaffolding command (socialagent init) creates the project structure and configuration around it. This file is where your agent logic lives.

The create_session_manager() function binds the agent to AgentCore memory scoped to that phone number, so history survives across sessions and deployments for the memory retention period (7 days by default).

In a recent development, the socialagent_notify_context() wrapper is the other pattern worth keeping. Tools sometimes need to send something while the agent is still working, such as a button list or a progress patch. Sending it immediately corrupts the conversation history, and the user’s next message fails. The wrapper collects those messages instead, and they go out in order once the turn finishes. Your tools send messages normally and do not deal with the timing.

The following diagram demonstrates how an inbound message travels from WhatsApp to your agent and back, and where the shared infrastructure sits.

Figure 1: How an inbound WhatsApp message flows through the SMART channel layer to the agent and back.

Industry observers note that the SMART core stack is organized into distinct layers: message processing, an agent layer, and a service layer. AWS End User Messaging Social receives inbound WhatsApp messages and routes them to the processing layer. An AWS Lambda function handles the channel logic, while Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the runtime, memory, and observability for the agent itself. Supporting services such as Amazon DynamoDB (optional, for per-user state), AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) supply state management, credentials, monitoring, and storage across the stack.

It has been revealed that inbound events arrive through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). On each event, the webhook Lambda function verifies the SNS message signature, normalizes the payload, and rate-limits each user (20 messages per minute by default, with the DynamoDB state table enabled). It then fires a read receipt and typing indicator, so the conversation feels alive before the model finishes. Voice notes go through Amazon Transcribe. Other media becomes a descriptor or goes to a hook you register if you want custom handling. When the agent throttles or fails, the user receives a readable message that you can customize, rather than silence.

Agents built on SMART interact directly with end users, so production deployments should include appropriate safeguards. The Terraform stack creates and configures an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails resource by default. With a single guardrail variable in your environment configuration, you can use the stack’s default guardrail, bring your own, or opt out entirely. The controls that you apply are up to you. SMART makes sure the wiring is already in place.

According to recent reports, after the message is ready, the webhook function passes it to AgentCore runtime. AgentCore memory maintains conversation context across sessions, and AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, traces every step for debugging and audit.

The webhook function sends the reply and messages your tools queued during the turn. A notification function handles sends outside a turn, such as proactive or scheduled messages. External systems trigger your event handlers by posting to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint protected by an API key and a Lambda authorizer. The event is published to Amazon SNS and the event Lambda runs your handler. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler handles time-based outreach, such as reminders and recurring check-ins. With message templates managed through AWS End User Messaging, you can send structured notifications outside the 24-hour WhatsApp session window.

A single socialagent deploy provisions the following resources (it runs terraform apply under the hood).

The agent container image and the Lambda layer build in AWS CodeBuild during the apply. Docker isn’t required locally.

Before you deploy, confirm that you have the following.

Note: This is sample code, for non-production usage. You should work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory and compliance requirements before deployment.

Start by cloning the repository and scaffolding a project.

The --blueprint flag selects a project blueprint. Three blueprints ship, and minimal is the default if you don’t pass an argument:.

Industry observers note that you get a project with your agent.py, socialagent.dev.yaml (the project’s deployment configuration), handler stubs for the webhook, notification, event, and scheduler paths, and a vendored copy of socialagent_runtime/. The personal assistant and appointment-scheduler blueprints also bring tools, skills, and a templates.yaml for your message templates. minimal ships none of those, so you add them as required.

Next, iterate locally, with no infrastructure at all.

The socialagent dev command runs your real agent loop and real tools in a terminal read-eval-print loop (REPL), with AWS channel I/O stubbed. Memory becomes a local file-backed session, and state becomes a local JSON file shared across your dev sessions. Notifications print to the terminal, including buttons and list rows. One-shot schedules run immediately. Recurring ones are registered but do not fire. Tool calls appear inline. The reply arrives as one message, as on WhatsApp. The /event and /schedule commands exercise the handler paths. No deployment is involved, so you can test a change as soon as you save it.

Industry observers note that two caveats apply. The model call is real, so a blueprint other than minimal needs AWS credentials and Amazon Bedrock access. The REPL also doesn’t simulate IAM or Meta’s template review. Testing through a deployed stack is highly recommended before you consider something done.

In a recent development, you can add capabilities as recipes. Each recipe is a plain Python function plus a markdown skill that teaches the agent when to use it.

Wiring the recipe to the agentic layer is the developer responsibility, which is what keeps recipes portable if you change agent frameworks.

When the behavior is right locally, deploy the stack.

One step Terraform cannot do for you. AWS End User Messaging Social needs to know where to deliver inbound messages. Point your WhatsApp Business Account at the Amazon SNS topic the stack created. That setting lives on the business account, not in the stack. Point the WABA’s event destination at the stack’s SNS topic using the admin console’s Bind action, or with aws socialmessaging put-whatsapp-business-account-event-destinations from the CLI. Until it is linked, inbound messages go nowhere, and nothing errors.

When the project includes a templates.yaml, the deploy step also syncs your message templates with Meta. If you need to sync templates independently, run uv run socialagent templates sync, which reads the phone number ID and prefix from socialagent.dev.yaml and the template definitions from templates.yaml. A rejected template will fail the deploy, so fix the wording before retrying.

According to recent reports, meta sorts templates by purpose, and a transactional one has more permissive sending rules than a promotional one. Keep the wording plain. Emojis and marketing language are the usual reason a template gets reclassified as promotional. Running templates sync --force re-registers every template, sending approved ones back through Meta review. A plain sync skips them. Leave approved templates alone unless you need to change their content.

Now you’re ready to message your WhatsApp number.

Shipping one bot is a project. Operating a fleet of them is the part nobody budgets for, so you also get an optional administration console with its own Terraform root. Deploy it once. Each SMART stack that sets admin_registry_bucket registers itself to a shared Amazon S3 registry on deploy, and the administration console discovers those stacks from there.

Sources indicate that the console gives you fleet health at a glance, then per-bot depth. From a single stack view, you can do the following.

The console also owns the phone-number binding described earlier, so rebinding a number to a different stack is a UI action.

Sign-in runs through Amazon Cognito, with multi-factor authentication (MFA) required. Role-based permissions are then enforced on every API route. The console itself is served from Amazon CloudFront over a private Amazon S3 bucket.

It has been revealed that the console runs on AWS services end to end. Every conversation stays within two providers: Meta and AWS. Model calls may be processed in other AWS Regions through Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference. See docs/data-flows.md in the repository for details on inference routing, media processing, and service opt-out options.

To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the stacks in the following order.

Terraform will not remove three things. The media and audit S3 buckets block destroy while they hold objects, unless enable_force_destroy is set. Templates registered with Meta persist. Your phone number registration is account-level and stays in place.

When building a WhatsApp AI product, the agent is where your differentiation lives. The channel integration is what eats your roadmap. SMART moves that boundary for you. Write a prompt, a few tools, and your business logic. In return you get webhook ingestion, media handling, conversation memory, scheduling, and template management. All backed by one-command infrastructure, a local development loop, and an administration console running in your own AWS account.

To go further, take the following next steps.

We would love to see what you build with it.

#2423. Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2196 w)

Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • It has been revealed that "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

It has been revealed that "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

Industry observers note that A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

It has been revealed that the community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

Recent findings suggest that we could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

Sources indicate that A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

Recent findings suggest that if we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Recent findings suggest that zero-shot classification addresses an vital part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

Industry observers note that this already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

It has been revealed that decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

In a recent development, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

According to recent reports, the state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

In a recent development, questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

Recent findings suggest that the model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

It has been revealed that ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Industry observers note that choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

It has been revealed that P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

In a recent development, the full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

According to recent reports, notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Recent findings suggest that our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

In a recent development, transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

It has been revealed that we can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Industry observers note that hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Recent findings suggest that once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it indicates the parts that matter:.

Recent findings suggest that first-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Recent findings suggest that traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Sources indicate that great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that states whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

Industry observers note that I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

#2420. Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally

Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators.
  • It has been revealed that every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works.
  • Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators.

It has been revealed that every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds.

The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole manufacturer. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads.

None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time.

Industry observers note that we rolled out AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built.

Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust.

Industry observers note that across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations.

Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over.

Industry observers note that without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each latest use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset.

Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. Newly introduced agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild.

Industry observers note that next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work.

The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down.

Sometimes the knowledge is buried in the systems themselves.

Recent findings suggest that rio Tinto Iron Ore runs one of the world’s most complex mine-to-ship supply chains on a 30-year-old Oracle system. That system has more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications. Mapping it had been a multi-month exercise. The FDE team built agents that mapped it in weeks, surfacing the dependencies that Rio Tinto’s teams could validate and build against.

Mapping what exists is only the start. The biggest opportunities emerge when organizations stop asking how AI can make existing work more efficient and start asking how it can change how work gets done.

Recent findings suggest that governance isn’t a phase of the project. It’s part of the architecture. As agents multiply, so do security risks, costs, and decisions you must explain. Every agent needs its own identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity. And because the models underneath are probabilistic, agents need monitoring that keeps their results predictable and auditable long after launch.

The system also must keep working as everything around it changes. Models drift, business rules shift, data formats change, and regulations tighten. New security concerns appear, and code falls out of date. As newer models arrive, the instructions and tooling around them will change too. You need evaluations and guardrails that keep agents predictable where they must be and creative where they can be.

When governance comes at the end, it becomes the gate that stops production. When it’s built in from day one, it’s what lets your business move fast.

In a recent development, marsh, a leading global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards. The FDE team built those controls in from the start, and the first use case reached production about two months after work began. Efficiency gains in the targeted areas have been as much as 70 percent, with some process steps moving from hours to seconds. Marsh has since expanded the work and keeps extending the system itself.

Our perspective comes from building and running these systems ourselves. AWS FDE pairs a small team of AWS engineers, scientists, and product managers with your engineers and a crew of specialized AI agents. Many of our FDEs come from the service teams that build Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, AWS Quick, and AWS Security Hub. They’ve built and run AI products at AWS scale, and they bring those engineering practices into your environment. Together, our teams take a high-value business problem to production in 45-day sprints, in your own AWS account. Customers shouldn’t need to choose between speed, scale, and control. FDE is built to deliver all three.

It has been revealed that speed – You might come to us with a broad goal or an ambiguous problem. We refine it with your business stakeholders, then build in your environment from day one, on your data and through your identity and security controls. We build in short cycles alongside the people who do the work. Each cycle puts real cases in front of them, and the unwritten rules come out as they react. We capture those rules in a living context, so the system keeps learning after we step back. Nothing gets rebuilt between prototype and production. You see working demos throughout, evaluations track progress against the outcomes you care about, and you have a production system within a quarter or less.

Scale – A point solution can move fast on one use case but leaves no foundation for the next five. Every FDE team works the same way, using the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), the method our own service teams use to take a broad problem to a working outcome. We deploy an opinionated AWS stack that reflects what we’ve learned building AI services, adapted to your environment: a living context of how your business works, a workbench where your engineers and agent crews build, a runtime on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and a control tower for governance, outcomes, cost, and agent performance. Accelerators for common tasks, such as document processing and customer sentiment analysis, handle the standard pieces, so each new workload can focus on what’s specific to your business. The opinionated AWS stack, context, and controls carry from one use case to the next.

Your context is what makes scaling possible. Say your first use case is a sales automation workflow. Because its context lives in your AWS account, the next use case, supply chain optimization, builds on it instead of starting over. Your context, tools, and AWS services all sit in one place, so each use case is faster to build than the last.

Control – You own what we build. Everything runs in your AWS account under your identity, network, and security controls. Your engineers work alongside ours from the first sprint, learning both the architecture and the delivery approach on a real business problem. They can then run and extend the solution long after the engagement ends. When we step back, your team runs the system from a control tower, a single view to govern, secure, and monitor every agent. We measure success by how much your team can build without us.

After the first or second project, we want you running AI software factories of your own. One financial services customer did exactly that with AI-DLC, with agents and engineers building together. Throughput rose 53%, and code reviews got 56% faster.

Sources indicate that you also keep your choices open. Models are improving fast. When a better or more cost-effective model arrives, you can adopt it through Amazon Bedrock without rebuilding, so you control both capability and cost. You can also bring your own coding agents. Our opinionated AWS stack, adapted to your environment, connects to your systems through APIs, open standards, and connectors, and it works in hybrid environments. You keep the tools and partners you already use.

Recent findings suggest that your team gets better. Your capability grows with every use case. The living context, the opinionated AWS stack, and your team’s skills carry forward, so the second use case doesn’t rebuild what the first one built.

Industry observers note that AWS Services get better. Our engineers bring what they learn from customers back into the products. You build on the latest services, not a custom solution that falls out of date.

It has been revealed that all of AWS works around you. Customer development engineering explores early ideas, FDE takes the hardest problems to production, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners extend the work across your organization, and AWS Support keeps it running. You get the full depth of AWS behind your AI, and you stay in control of how you use it.

AWS FDE is now available in 15 countries to commercial and public sector customers, and it’s simpler to buy. Each 45-day sprint has a set price under the FDE Terms and is billed through your AWS account.

Sources indicate that we work with customers wherever they are in their transformation. For customers starting out, we build a secure, governed foundation and the first workflows on it. For those ready to change how work gets done, we rebuild workflows such as claims processing and KYC reviews, along with the ones their customers use directly, like shopping and issue resolution. Agents then run the work. For those held back by legacy applications, we work with their engineers to build software factories they can reuse for each new workflow. For those already scaling in production, we keep systems secure with agents that find and fix concerns, and we lower the cost per outcome.

If you’re ready to start, talk with your AWS account team. Bring an executive who owns the outcome and engineers ready to build alongside ours. We’ve learned where projects stall before they start, so our agents take on much of the setup, like access, data, and security checks. Work can begin within days. Then we agree together on what the first sprint will deliver and how we’ll measure success.

The gap between AI that works and AI that changes business outcomes is real. It is an engineering, operational, and organizational one, and our teams help customers close it every day. The organizations that succeed with AI won’t necessarily have the most advanced models. They’ll be the ones that build the foundation, workflows, and governance to scale AI across the business.

Sources indicate that we’re still early, and we learn something new with every customer. The models will continue to evolve, and so will the tools around them. What should last is a foundation you own, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. That’s what we mean by what remains after our engineers leave.

To get started, contact your AWS account team or learn more about AWS FDE.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CISA has added two latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

According to recent reports, you can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your organization already runs on Google Cloud, adding a latest vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

According to recent reports, you are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now highlights the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

It has been revealed that once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Industry observers note that thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

Subnet Solutions reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. These vulnerabilities are not exploitable remotely. Breaking: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data.
  • In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project.
  • Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with upcoming AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference.

In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models.

Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with upcoming AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change.

According to recent reports, with AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want.

It has been revealed that you work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice.

Industry observers note that for teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product.

It has been revealed that “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.”.

— Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability.

Sources indicate that the value grows when you combine the capabilities. Some common patterns:.

Build a golden evaluation dataset: Auto-label your raw data from a small seed set. High-confidence rows are accepted automatically, and low-confidence rows go to human reviewers. Their corrections improve the next labeling pass, resulting in a trusted, human-validated dataset to benchmark your models against.

Go from raw documents to a trained model in one workflow:.

Consider a team preparing data to evaluate agentic customer support assistants. Its product guide indicates that a factory reset erases saved settings. The team wants to test whether the assistant preserves that warning when answering reset questions.

One pass through the preparation workflow looks like this:.

This example workflow illustrates how the capabilities fit together.

With the AI-ML skill, you describe the task in natural language while your coding agent helps build specifications, prepare code, and coordinate the data preparation steps. You can open those artifacts to see how the workflow is configured and make changes directly.

Recent findings suggest that if you prefer to invoke the APIs yourself, use the Python SDK APIs to call individual capabilities from your own code. The SDK APIs take a specification as input, so we recommend creating it with the help of an agent. You can add quality assessment to an existing process, generate data for a newly introduced task, or combine several operations. You choose the preparation steps your project needs and how they fit into your model customization and evaluation processes.

AI Data Preparation runs with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you control. Your source data, generated datasets, and labels stay in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, in the AWS Region you choose.

In a recent development, the AI data preparation capabilities are generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. #2402. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1989 w)
